thinking_and_logic: The final logic collects indices where nums[i] equals target. Two Sum instead requires finding two distinct indices (i, j) such that nums[i] + nums[j] == target. This mismatch explains why tests expecting pairs like [0,1] or cases with negatives/duplicates all returned []. The canonical reasoning is: for each element x at index i, the needed partner is (target - x); if that needed value was seen earlier, you’ve found the answer.
code_assessment: Compared to the answer key’s optimal solution (single pass + hash map of seen value->index), your code does not attempt pairing or complement lookup, so it cannot solve the intended problem. It also accumulates potentially multiple indices, whereas the prompt guarantees exactly one valid pair and typical solutions return immediately when found. Implementing the hash-map complement pattern would address correctness and still meet the constraints (n up to 1e5) efficiently.

next_steps.action: Practice the one-pass hash map 'complement lookup' pattern for Two Sum and similar problems
next_steps.why: It is the canonical optimal approach here (O(n) time, O(n) space) and directly prevents the common missteps around duplicates and index reuse.
next_steps.how: Implement: seen = {}; for i,x in enumerate(nums): need=target-x; if need in seen: return [seen[need], i]; seen[x]=i. Then test on: [2,7,11,15],9; [3,3],6; [-1,-2,-3,-4,-5],-8.
